title: The day every place gets 12 hours
hook: Summer days are long in the north and winter days short. Is there a day when that stops?

knows: that summer has long days and winter short ones
latitude in degrees north of the equator
doesNotKnow: that at the equinox every latitude gets about 12 hours of daylight
why day length depends on latitude only when the Sun is off the equator

misconception: Even at the equinox, places far from the equator get longer or shorter days than the tropics.
objective: The learner can explain that at the equinox the day-night line runs pole to pole, so every parallel is half lit (about 12 hours at 60°N as at the equator), and that the tilt makes day length depend on latitude on other dates.

claims.text: On the March equinox the Sun is above the horizon for about 12 hours at 60°N, the same as at the equator.
claims.source: Day length from cos H = -tan φ tan δ (Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms, ch. 15; from memory). At δ = 0, H = 90° for every φ < 90°, so 2H/15° = 12.000 h. Computed in Demo.tsx dayHours, the same function that draws the lit part of the line. Geometric day: Sun's centre on the horizon, no refraction. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: cos H = -tan(lat) tan(dec) at dec = 0 gives H = 90 deg, 12.000 h at 0N and 60N (geometric day, Sun's centre).

claims.text: At the equinox the line between day and night runs from pole to pole, so every line of latitude is half lit.
claims.source: With the subsolar point on the equator, the terminator is the great circle 90° from it, which passes through both poles (a pair of meridians). Drawn by nightPolygons in Demo.tsx. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): With the subsolar point on the equator the terminator is the great circle 90 deg away, through both poles; every parallel is cut into equal halves (node: 12 h at all latitudes).

claims.text: On the equinox the Sun is overhead at the equator; on other dates the Earth's tilt puts it north or south of the equator.
claims.source: Definition of the equinox (Sun's declination 0) and obliquity 23.44° (Astronomical Almanac; from memory, not checked online). The stage uses a simple model, declination = -23.44° cos(angle round the orbit) at five dates 1/8 year apart; 'early Feb' and 'early May' are model dates (declination ±16.6°), not almanac values. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Equinox = Sun's declination 0 and over the equator; obliquity 23.44 deg (23.4393 at J2000). Stage model dec = -23.44 cos(45 i deg): -23.44, -16.57, 0, +16.57, +23.44 for the five dates; early Feb / early May are model dates, labelled as such.

claims.text: On 21 June the same formula gives about 18.5 hours of daylight at 60°N.
claims.source: cos H = -tan 60° tan 23.44° = -0.751, H = 138.7°, 2H/15 = 18.5 h. Shown in the reveal only if the learner looked at 60°N on 21 June. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: cos H = -tan60 tan23.44 = -0.751, H = 138.7 deg, 18.49 h at 60N (geometric). With the standard -0.833 deg sunrise definition the real value is about 18.9 h; the stage states 'Geometric day' in its footer.

claims.text: Real equinox days run a few minutes over 12 hours, because air bends sunlight and the Sun is a disc, not a point.
claims.source: Sunrise and sunset are defined by the Sun's upper limb with about 34' of refraction (US Naval Observatory definition, -0.833° altitude; from memory, not checked online). The brief's check gives about 7 minutes extra at the equator and 13 at 60°N; the lesson says 'a few minutes' and shows no number. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: with the standard -0.833 deg altitude of the Sun's upper limb, the equinox day is 6.7 min over 12 h at the equator and 13.3 min at 60N. Non-blocking wording note: 'a few minutes' fits the equator better than 60N, the lesson's key latitude; 'up to a quarter of an hour' would be closer.

claims.text: Oslo and Helsinki lie at about 60°N.
claims.source: Oslo 59.9°N, Helsinki 60.2°N (any gazetteer; from memory). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Oslo 59.91N and Helsinki 60.17N (standard gazetteer values); 'about 60N' holds.

recall.question: On the September equinox, which place gets the most hours of daylight: Quito (equator), Rome (42°N) or Oslo (60°N)?
recall.why: At an equinox the Sun is over the equator and the day-night line runs pole to pole, so every latitude is half lit: about 12 hours everywhere.
